chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from his father, from Khalaf ibn Hammad, from one of his companions, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

By Allah, performing one Hajj is more beloved to me than freeing one slave, and another, and another, and a similar one, and a similar one until it reaches ten, and a similar one, and a similar one until it reaches seventy; and looking after a family from the Muslims, satisfying their hunger, and clothing their nakedness, so that it would preserve their faces from the people, is more beloved to me than if I were to perform one Hajj, and another, and another, and a similar one, and a similar one until it reaches ten, and a similar one, and a similar one until it reaches seventy.

key_terms.أَكُفَّ وُجُوهَهُمْ: To preserve their faces (dignity) from people
key_terms.عَوْرَتَهُمْ: Their nakedness or need for clothing

ai.seo_question: What is more beloved to the Imam: performing many Hajjs or supporting a poor family?
ai.summary: In this hadith from al-Kafi, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) elevates the practical act of sustaining a Muslim family’s dignity above the cumulative merit of seventy Hajjs or freeing seventy slaves, highlighting the Shia emphasis on social welfare as a superior form of worship. This comparison underscores the concept of 'kaf al-awrah' (covering the nakedness/shame) through financial independence, linking material support directly to spiritual purification. The narration reflects the broader Shia scholarly tradition that views relieving the distress of believers as a means of drawing closer to God, often equated with or surpassing individual acts of devotion.
